title: Zomato Founder Deepinder Goyal's 'Temple' Wearable Tracks Brain Blood Flow, Priced Around ₹75,000
excerpt: The pill-shaped device, worn between the forehead and the ear, uses optical sensing to track cerebral blood flow; waitlist pre-orders open soon ahead of shipments before end-2026.
body:
• Temple is a pill-shaped wearable worn between the forehead and the ear that tracks cerebral blood flow via its BrainFlow optical sensing system.
  • The device uses photoplethysmography (PPG), not EEG — it measures blood-volume changes in tissue near the temple, not electrical brain activity.
  • Developed by Goyal-backed Continue Research with collaborators at IISc, IIT Bombay and SISSA Trieste, Temple is expected to cost around ₹72,000–₹80,000, with waitlist pre-orders opening soon and shipments before end-2026.
  • For buyers: Goyal says the disposable adhesive "Grips" fit 99% of users, stay on through swimming and showers, and come in unlimited supply with the purchase.

Deepinder Goyal wants to move the wearable from the wrist to the temple. The Zomato founder's health-tech project, a compact device called Temple, tracks physiological signals associated with blood flow to the brain — a health metric no mainstream wearable measures continuously today. Pre-orders for users on the early-access waitlist could open as early as next week, with shipments expected before the end of 2026.

What Temple is

Temple is a small, pill-shaped device worn on the side of the head, between the forehead and the ear, secured with disposable adhesive tapes called Grips. Its core technology, BrainFlow, uses photoplethysmography (PPG) — an optical sensing method also used in the Apple Watch — to detect changes in blood volume in tissue near the temple. Goyal has been explicit that Temple is not an EEG device: it does not record electrical brain activity and cannot diagnose medical conditions. Instead, it is designed to track how factors such as sleep, exercise, stress and cold exposure relate to cerebral blood flow.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=E0j7B4WAGxU

A 60-participant validation study compared BrainFlow measurements against time-domain near-infrared spectroscopy (TD-NIRS), a technique that can distinguish blood-volume changes in brain tissue from scalp-level signals. The research has been submitted for peer review, and Goyal has encouraged independent researchers to test the technology — a notably open posture for a consumer device.

The design details

The Grips were, by Goyal's account, as hard to engineer as the device itself: "Inventing the right Grips was as hard as making the device," he wrote on X, saying the final version works for 99% of users and that the purchase price includes an unlimited supply. The device is designed to stay put through running, swimming, sauna and showers — everything except scuba diving — with a battery life of about seven days; the company recommends swapping the Grip every two to three days.

The launch edition will come in six colours: True Gold, Rose Gold, Black Mirror, Real Jade, Deep Blue and Purple Funk. The expected price is around ₹72,000 to ₹80,000, positioning Temple as a luxury health product rather than a mass-market tracker. It is being developed through Continue Research, a Goyal-backed initiative separate from Zomato's parent Eternal, with scientific collaborators at IISc, IIT Bombay and Italy's SISSA Trieste.

The visibility campaign

Goyal first showcased Temple on Raj Shamani's podcast, and badminton star PV Sindhu has been seen wearing it in competition — an endorsement money cannot buy in Indian sport. On X this week, Goyal went further, saying he "certainly would have it on pilots" and suggesting the Indian Air Force could use it to determine who is fittest for a given mission — though the device is not approved or certified for aviation safety.

Analysis: ambition and risk

Temple is Goyal's second attempt at building outside food delivery, and it is a genuinely novel category: cerebral blood flow is a real but rarely measured signal, and the brain's 20%-of-blood-supply claim Goyal cites is standard physiology. The risks are equally real. At ₹75,000-plus, this is priced for early adopters and the quantified-self wealthy; the leap from a 60-person validation study to consumer-grade medical relevance is enormous; and consumer PPG near the temple will face scepticism from clinicians until the peer-reviewed data lands.

That Goyal is inviting independent testing before launch suggests he knows the credibility battle is the product. If BrainFlow's validation holds up, Temple could open a new lane in health wearables. If it doesn't, it joins the long list of brain-health gadgets that promised more than optics could deliver.

What's next

Pre-orders for the waitlist, the final price, and the peer-review outcome are the three near-term markers. Watch whether the study passes review — and whether clinicians, not just tech enthusiasts, start paying attention.
